newsitem.title: USA: Plan to defer CRP for Yellowstone mine draws fire.
newsitem.headline: Plan to defer CRP for Yellowstone mine draws fire.

text.p: An administration plan to offset the costs of stopping mining near Yellowstone National Park by deferring the enrollment of two million acres into the Agriculture Department's Conservation Reserve Program has drawn criticism from agricultural groups and some lawmakers.

The White House announced Wednesday that it has offered to pay Crown Butte Mines $65 million to not develop a mine near the famous national park. The money will come from coal, oils and natural gas royalty revenue over several years, but the loss to the Treasury will be offset by delaying for one year the enrollment of two million acres into the CRP.
Farm interests said it was not right that a popular farm program should have to help cover the costs of an unrelated federal expense.

"We would have a big concern about taking money from CRP to pay for this mine," said Rosemary Watkins of the American Farm Bureau Federation. "If they need to deal with that, they need to come up with money from the appropriate program, not raid another successful program."
The plan has to be approved by Congress, where some lawmakers said it could run into trouble, in part because of the plan to involve the CRP.
A spokesman for Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman Ricahrd Lugar (R-Ind) predicted that the proposal could hit some snags in the appropriations committees.
"That's a pretty big leap -- to draw CRP (money) for a project that is out of the agricultural area and more in the natural resources area," said the Lugar aide.
A spokesman for Montana republican Senator Conrad Burns said the administration is trying to "solve the problem on the backs of farmers."
Signup for the Agriculture Department's newest CRP program version is underway throughout the nation, and USDA officials said activity has been brisk.
The department has been aggressively promoting the program, and has said it is committed to maintaining an enrollment of 36 million acres of fragile land in the CRP.
A USDA spokesman said the proposed enrollment deferral is in no way an attempt to weaken the program.
"We have two important competing priorities, and we believe we can do both. There is absolutely no weakening of our committment to the CRP program," said USDA press secretary Tom Amontree.

An administration source said that according to an internal fact sheet on the proposal, the administration stressed that it has not cut the program, and that the 36 million acres remains the overall target.

Current White House budget projections allow for 19 million acres of cropland to be freshly enrolled in the program this year and 8 million the following year. Under the proposed deferrel, only 17 million acres of cropland would be accepted into CRP this year, and 10 million next year.
"This is just changing the curve of the enrollment. From our sense, there's nothing about this that compromises the CRP," said a White House source.
